proposedDescription: Buckwheat grows quickly into a soft, branching annual with arrowhead-shaped leaves and clusters of small white or pink-tinged flowers. Although its seeds are used like grain, it belongs to the knotweed family rather than the grasses. Farmers also grow it as a short-season cover crop, where its dense growth shades weeds and its flowers draw bees and other beneficial insects. Plants sometimes appear outside cultivation, especially on disturbed ground; that alone does not establish an invasive impact.
identification: Alternate arrowhead-shaped leaves, hollow stems that may redden, and clusters of five-parted white flowers.
actions: Where volunteers are unwanted, remove plants before mature seed forms; retain planted cover crops according to the growing plan.
researchNotes: Both accounts read. Removal before seeding is preventive advice, not a claim of species-specific eradication. No ecological invasiveness claim.

claims: Fast-growing summer annual in knotweed family; leaves, hollow stems, white flowers and beneficial insects.
Grain-like crop and cover-crop uses; establishment and weed-management context.

proposedDescription: The Budapest slug is a slender, ground-dwelling slug often found around gardens, cultivated fields and other disturbed places. Its brownish-gray body is densely speckled, with a pale yellow ridge running down the tail. A dark stripe along the otherwise pale underside is especially useful when separating it from similar keeled slugs. It can feed both above and below the soil surface, damaging root crops, bulbs and newly sown seed. A curled, horseshoe-like resting posture is another helpful clue.
identification: Usually 4-6 cm long; pale tail keel, spotted gray-brown body and a dark central stripe on the sole.
actions: Photograph the back and underside for identification, and inspect bulbs and root crops where feeding damage occurs.

sources.title: John Innes Centre: Budapest keeled slug

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts were opened and read. No county occurrence or nationwide invasive status is inferred.

claims: Size, tail keel, sole stripe, below-ground feeding and crop damage.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Conchological Society of Great Britain and Ireland
claims: Color, spots, keel, underside and garden/crop habitat.

proposedDescription: Buff coconut mealybugs look rather like tiny wax-covered cushions on their host plants. Adult females are orange to reddish brown, with yellowish wax and pointed tufts around the edge and across the back. Despite the common name, they feed on many plants, including palms, avocado and ornamental flowers. Their sap feeding produces sticky honeydew that can support black sooty mold, and ants may tend the colonies. Close inspection of a mature female is often needed to confirm the species.
identification: Oval females about 1.5-2.5 mm long, with yellow-orange wax and pyramid-shaped tufts; males form small white cocoons.
actions: Inspect leaf undersides and stems, isolate suspect nursery plants, and obtain a confirmed identification before choosing treatment.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts were opened and read. No county occurrence or nationwide invasive status is inferred.

claims: Female morphology, broad host range, sap feeding, honeydew, ants and inspection.
Coconut mealybug hosts and distinctive yellow wax with pyramidal tufts.

proposedDescription: Buffelgrass forms coarse perennial clumps with rough leaves and fuzzy, bottlebrush-shaped seed heads. Originally planted as forage in dry regions, it is a serious problem in the Sonoran Desert, where it fills the spaces between native shrubs and cacti. Those connected patches carry fire through vegetation that is poorly adapted to burning. The seed heads change from reddish or purplish tones to tan as they mature, and seeds can travel on shoes, clothing, animals and moving water.
identification: Coarse bunchgrass with rough bluish-green leaves and dense cylindrical, bristly seed heads that turn tan.
actions: Clean seeds from footwear and equipment. Report new desert patches and join trained local removal efforts; follow up for regrowth.

sources.title: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum: Save our saguaros

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts were opened and read. No county occurrence or nationwide invasive status is inferred.

claims: Perennial bunchgrass, leaf and seed-head traits, and seed dispersal.
Buffelgrass connects fuels and spreads destructive desert fires; organized removal events.

proposedDescription: Bukhara fleeceflower, also called silver lace vine, can cover a fence with a cloud of tiny pale flowers in late summer. This deciduous, twining climber has heart-shaped leaves and woody older stems. Its speed is part of its appeal in gardens, but also the reason it needs careful placement: shoots can scramble across nearby shrubs and quickly outgrow their support. Small winged fruits develop after flowering, often taking on a pink or reddish tint.
identification: Twining woody vine with alternate heart-shaped leaves and loose masses of small white to pinkish flowers.
actions: Keep cultivated vines within their support with regular pruning, and remove unwanted growth before it spreads over neighboring plants.

sources.title: University of Arkansas Extension: Silver lace vine

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Twining perennial habit, vigorous growth, heart-shaped leaves, flowering and winged fruits.
Deciduous woody climber, pink-white flowers, fruit and pruning requirement.

proposedDescription: The bulb and potato aphid lives in places that are easy to overlook: around roots, inside stored bulbs and on potato tubers. It feeds on a wide range of plants, including ornamental bulbs such as tulips and gladiolus, and can affect crops both in the field and in storage. It is also associated with transmission of plant viruses. Because colonies may remain hidden below ground, careful inspection of planting material is more useful than looking only at the leaves.
identification: Look for aphid colonies on roots, bulbs and tubers; species confirmation requires an aphid specialist rather than host plant alone.
actions: Inspect stored bulbs and seed potatoes before planting or sharing them, and keep suspect material separate while seeking identification.

sources.title: Petrovic-Obradovic and colleagues: First record in Serbia

researchNotes: AphID full account and independent research abstract read; linked full paper failed to load. Broad host wording follows the paper, avoiding AphID's internally contradictory 'narrow' range sentence. Inspection advice is preventive.

claims: Bulb, tuber and root feeding; ornamental hosts; field and storage importance; virus associations.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Entomological Society of Serbia primary research
claims: Cryptic root, bulb and tuber feeding; winged specimens collected during field monitoring.

proposedDescription: Bulbil bugle-lily sends tall spikes of curved, trumpet-shaped flowers above fans of tough, swordlike leaves. This South African perennial grows from underground corms and is familiar in gardens for its salmon, pink, red or pale blooms. The bulbil-producing form develops small brown cormlets along the flower stems, each capable of starting another plant. In invaded open habitats, dense clumps can crowd out other vegetation; moving soil or dumping garden waste can carry the corms to new sites.
identification: Swordlike basal leaves and tall tubular-flowered spikes; inspect stems for brown bulbils in the bulbil-producing form.
actions: Keep corms and bulbils out of dumped garden waste. For small unwanted clumps, carefully collect underground corms and stem bulbils and monitor regrowth.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Watsonia meriana

researchNotes: Species-wide morphology separated from Weedbusters' Bulbillifera form. Its New Zealand no-seed statement is not generalized to the entire species.

claims: Corm-forming clumps, sword-shaped leaves, flower structure and color variation.
Bulbillifera morphology, vegetative reproduction, spread in soil and waste, dense infestations.

proposedDescription: Bulbous bluegrass is a small, cool-season grass that gets an early start in spring and dries out early as conditions warm. It grows in tufts, with narrow leaves ending in the little boat-shaped tips typical of bluegrasses. Many plants carry an unusual flowering head full of tiny leafy bulblets, rather than an ordinary-looking spray of seeds. These bulblets and the swollen bases of the shoots help it persist and spread. It occurs on disturbed ground and has also been used to stabilize eroding soil.
identification: Small bunchgrass with boat-tipped leaves, swollen basal shoots and often sprouting bulblets in the flower head.
actions: Photograph both the plant base and flowering head. Avoid carrying bulblets in soil or equipment when working through a patch.

sources.title: University of Illinois Extension: Bulbous bluegrass

researchNotes: Two independent accounts read. Preventing movement is conservative containment advice; no claim of eradication.

claims: Short bunchgrass, boat-tipped leaves, membranous ligule and disturbed-ground habitat.
Cool-season perennial; early growth and curing; basal bulbs and reproductive bulblets; erosion-seeding history.

proposedDescription: Bulbous canarygrass, often called Harding grass, is a robust perennial that forms tall, leafy clumps topped by dense cylindrical flower heads. Slightly swollen shoot bases give it its other common name. Introduced from Mediterranean Europe as a forage grass, it has escaped into fields, ditches and streamside habitats. In affected western landscapes, established clumps compete with native vegetation for water and space. Most new plants arise from seed, although pieces of its short underground stems can also regrow.
identification: Coarse clumps with broad grass blades, swollen shoot bases, a membranous ligule and dense spike-like flower heads.
actions: Remove small unwanted patches with follow-up checks; avoid cultivating established clumps into fragments, which can regrow.

sources.title: Flora of New Zealand: Phalaris aquatica

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Forage introduction, habitat, competitive clumps, seed and rhizome reproduction, mechanical management limits.
Strong perennial clumps with short knotted rhizomes, tuberous shoot bases and leaf morphology.

proposedDescription: Bull thistle starts as a low rosette of prickly leaves, then raises a branching stem with pinkish-purple flower heads. Unlike creeping thistles, it has a taproot and spreads by seed. The leaves are rough and hairy above, woolly beneath, and tipped with sharp spines; spiny wings also run down the stems. Originally from Eurasia, it readily colonizes disturbed soil and heavily grazed ground. Its prickles discourage grazing and can make neighboring forage harder for animals to reach.
identification: Spiny-winged stems, coarse prickly leaves with woolly undersides, and large purple heads surrounded by sharp bracts.
actions: Confirm the identification against native thistles. Remove small rosettes below the soil surface before flowering and revisit for seedlings.

sources.title: University of Nevada Extension: Bull thistle
University of Florida: Thistle control in pastures

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Biennial rosette, taproot, spiny wings, flowers, seed reproduction and grazing impacts.
Identification key distinguishes bull thistle; early rosette removal and seed prevention.

proposedDescription: Bur chervil has delicate, fernlike leaves, but its small hooked fruits are its most useful calling card. This Eurasian herb commonly grows as an annual, with hollow, branching stems and little clusters of white flowers beside the upper leaves. The burrlike fruits catch on animals and help the plant travel beyond the parent patch. In parts of the western United States it can form dense growth along waterways and beneath shrubs, although it also survives in drier grassland.
identification: Finely divided leaves, small white flower umbels beside upper leaves, and short oval fruits covered in hooked hairs.
actions: Photograph ripe fruits for a reliable identification. Pull small confirmed patches before seed ripens and brush burrs from clothing and equipment.

sources.title: University of California: Bur and wild chervil
University of British Columbia E-Flora: Bur chervil

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Annual habit, axillary white umbels, hooked fruit, animal dispersal, regional habitat and hand pulling.
Taproot, branching stems, divided leaves and small lateral flower clusters.

proposedDescription: Burmann's basketgrass is a low annual grass with spreading stems and relatively broad leaves. The blades can look gently rippled across their width, a useful clue when the plant is not flowering. Its flower head is arranged as several short branches along a central stalk, with slender, often pinkish-red bristles extending well beyond the tiny spikelets. It can grow beside paths and in other disturbed places. Similar basketgrasses need careful comparison, especially when assessing a plant outside its familiar range.
identification: Broad lance-shaped leaves, low spreading stems and short flower branches with long reddish awns.
actions: Photograph leaves, stems and mature flower heads for botanical confirmation before removing an unfamiliar basketgrass.

sources.title: University of Richmond Kaxil Kiuic flora: Oplismenus burmannii

researchNotes: Two botanical descriptions read. No US origin, invasive impact or control-efficacy claim is supported by these sources; none is made.

claims: Annual prostrate habit, broad leaves and racemes with long rough awns.
Annual habit, transversely undulate leaves and pinkish-red awns; path-edge example.

proposedDescription: Burmese fishtail palm gets its name from the jagged, fan-shaped leaflets that resemble little fish tails. Several slender trunks grow together in a clump, with new shoots arising at the base. Flowering follows an unusual sequence: a trunk flowers near its top first, then progressively lower down, and dies after its final flowering. The rest of the clump continues growing. Native to tropical Asia, this palm is widely cultivated in warm climates; its small fruits contain irritating material and should not be handled casually.
identification: Clustered smooth trunks and large, twice-divided leaves with broad, ragged-edged fishtail leaflets.
actions: Avoid handling crushed fruit; wear gloves when cleaning beneath plants and keep fruit away from children and pets.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Clumping habit, distinctive leaflets, flowering sequence, trunk death and irritating fruits.
Fishtail palm horticultural form, cultivation and fruit characteristics.

proposedDescription: Burclover spreads low across the ground, with three-parted leaves that can easily be mistaken for an ordinary clover. Small yellow flowers give way to tightly coiled pods, often armed with hooks that cling to fur and clothing. It grows in lawns, fields, roadsides and other disturbed places, and is also grown as forage or a cover crop. The same burrs that help disperse its seeds can become tangled in sheep's wool, reducing its value.
identification: Three rounded leaflets with toothed margins, small yellow pea-shaped flowers and coiled, prickly pods.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before the pods harden and detach; check clothing and animal coats for burrs after crossing a patch.
researchNotes: Identification and biology supported independently. Pre-seed removal is preventive advice, not a sourced eradication guarantee.

claims: Trifoliate leaves, yellow flowers, sprawling stems and coiled burr fruits.
Annual disturbed-ground plant, forage and cover-crop use, and wool contamination.

proposedDescription: Burmese pythons are large, muscular snakes patterned with dark, irregular patches on a tan background. They are comfortable in water and can be remarkably difficult to notice among wetland plants. Native to Southeast Asia, they have an established invasive population in southern Florida, where they eat a wide variety of mammals, birds and reptiles. Their broad diet is well documented: one study of digestive contents from more than 1,700 Florida pythons identified 76 prey species.
identification: Large tan snake with dark puzzle-piece blotches and a dark arrow-shaped marking on the head; do not approach for a closer look.
actions: Keep a safe distance, record the location and a photo if possible, and report suspected Florida sightings through the state wildlife reporting system.

sources.title: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Burmese python
USGS: Diet of invasive Burmese pythons, 1995-2020

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
claims: Body markings, head pattern, semi-aquatic habitat, Florida status and public reporting.
Digestive tracts of 1716 pythons contained 76 species of birds, mammals and reptiles.

proposedDescription: Bushkiller is a vigorous vine that uses tendrils to climb over shrubs, trees and garden structures. Its leaves have five toothed leaflets, and the small flowers are orange or salmon colored. The fleshy roots send up new shoots, particularly after they are disturbed, helping a patch recover even when the visible vines have been cut back. Native to Asia, Australia and nearby Pacific regions, it has escaped cultivation in the southern United States and is considered invasive in North Carolina.
identification: Climbing tendrils, alternate leaves divided into five shiny, serrated leaflets, and small orange-salmon flowers.
actions: Avoid moving root pieces in soil or garden waste. Seek a site-specific removal plan and revisit cut patches for new shoots.
researchNotes: NC State uses Causonis japonica; exact catalog ID and taxon preserved. No unverified seed-spread claim.

claims: Tendrils, fleshy roots, disturbance-induced shoots, five leaflets and vegetative spread.
Cayratia synonym, native range, perennial climbing habit and North Carolina invasiveness.

proposedDescription: Bushy yate is an evergreen eucalypt from Western Australia that grows as a bushy small tree or a many-stemmed mallee. Its smooth bark varies from pale pink and gray-brown to reddish tones, sometimes with older bark collected around the base. Cream, greenish or yellow flowers add a softer contrast to the foliage. In its native landscape it grows on exposed slopes, rocky outcrops, coastal dunes and creek beds; it is also planted as an ornamental tree elsewhere.
identification: Bushy evergreen eucalypt with smooth, variably pink-gray bark and cream to green-yellow flowers; compare buds and fruit with a regional key.
actions: Record flowers, buds and woody fruit for identification before managing a self-sown eucalypt; common names can cover similar species.

sources.title: Botanic Gardens of South Australia: Bushy yate

researchNotes: No invasive impact is inferred from cultivation outside its native range. Avoided traits belonging to similarly named E. conferruminata.

claims: Native Western Australian mallee, height, bark, flower colors and habitat.
Evergreen small tree, smooth trunk, green flowers and ornamental use.

proposedDescription: Butter and eggs is the familiar yellow toadflax, with pale yellow, snapdragon-shaped flowers and a deeper orange-yellow center. Slender leaves line its upright stems, and each flower carries a long spur at the back. Once grown as an ornamental and dye plant, it now occurs along roadsides, in fields and in other open ground across much of temperate North America. A spreading root system lets it form persistent patches, making a few flowering stems part of a much larger plant.
identification: Narrow alternate leaves and two-toned yellow snapdragon flowers with long backward-pointing spurs.
actions: Check wildflower mixtures before sowing. Remove small unwanted patches with their roots and monitor for regrowth; repeated management is usually needed.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Butter and eggs

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Eurasian origin, ornamental and dye history, open disturbed habitats and spreading growth.
Spreading roots, narrow alternate leaves, snapdragon flowers and long spur.

proposedDescription: Butterfly tree is also known as purple orchid-tree, and both names fit: its rounded leaves are split into two lobes, while its showy flowers range from pink to deep purple. This small to medium tree comes from India and Myanmar and is widely planted in warm regions. Long, flat seedpods follow the flowers and may remain on the branches through winter. In Florida it has escaped cultivation and is considered invasive, so its ornamental appeal needs to be weighed against local spread.
identification: Two-lobed, butterfly-shaped leaves; large pink-purple flowers and long, flat brown pods.
actions: In regions where it is invasive, choose an alternative tree and remove unwanted seedlings before they mature and produce pods.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Native India-Myanmar range, tree form, butterflylike leaves and pink-purple flowers.
Flowering, long persistent pods, cultivation and Florida invasive assessment.

proposedDescription: Butternut canker fungus attacks the bark of butternut trees, creating dead, sunken areas that can gradually encircle branches and trunks. Early damage may appear around leaf scars or wounds; older cankers become long cracks or open, dark-stained patches edged with ridges of living bark. As the disease advances, branches die back and the crown thins. Spores move between trees in rain splash and by other carriers. The disease has caused severe losses of butternut across its eastern North American range.
identification: On butternut, look for expanding branch dieback, dark sunken cankers, cracked bark and black-brown stained wood; laboratory confirmation may be needed.
actions: Ask a tree-health specialist to assess suspected cankers. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts and retain apparently healthy butternuts for conservation review.

sources.title: University of Minnesota: Butternut branch dieback

researchNotes: Minnesota uses the older Sirococcus name; Wisconsin explicitly confirms the catalog's Ophiognomonia name. No treatment cure is claimed.

claims: Causal fungus, canker development, girdling, spore movement and sanitation.
Progressive crown dieback, cracks, oval cankers and stained wood; older Sirococcus name.

proposedDescription: Button burrweed stays close to the ground, forming small patches of finely divided, fernlike leaves. Its flowers are easy to miss because the heads sit together near the plant's center rather than rising on showy stalks. As the fruits mature, the clusters become buttonlike and woolly, with stiff pointed tips. This South American annual has become established in disturbed ground and pastures elsewhere. Mature fruit is especially useful for separating it from other small burrweeds with a similar leafy appearance.
identification: Low rosette with deeply divided leaves and clustered, woolly fruiting heads near the base; fruits have a stiff terminal spine.
actions: Photograph mature heads for confirmation, then remove unwanted plants before burrs scatter; wear gloves when handling fruiting patches.

sources.title: New South Wales Flora Online: Soliva anthemifolia
Flora of New Zealand: Soliva anthemifolia

researchNotes: No lawn-control guidance for S. sessilis has been transferred to this species. Removal before dispersal is preventive advice.

claims: Annual prostrate herb, divided basal leaves and clustered flower heads.
South American origin, waste-ground/pasture habitat, woolly heads and fruit distinctions from S. sessilis.

proposedDescription: Busy lizzy is a soft-stemmed tropical perennial best known as a colorful bedding plant for shady gardens. Compact mounds of glossy foliage carry flowers in white, pink, red, orange and many cultivated combinations, often from late spring until frost. In colder climates it is usually grown as an annual. Ripe capsules release their seeds suddenly, giving the genus its 'impatient' name. Common garden impatiens can suffer from downy mildew, which yellows the leaves and may leave plants nearly bare.
identification: Fleshy branching stems, toothed oval leaves and flat five-petaled flowers, sometimes doubled in cultivated varieties.
actions: Keep garden waste out of natural areas. If plants develop downy mildew, remove infected material and do not place it in a home compost pile.
researchNotes: Catalog common-name spelling preserved by ID; prose uses standard Busy lizzy. No nationwide invasive claim.

claims: Tropical perennial grown as annual, flower colors, mounding habit and explosive seed release.
Glossy foliage, garden use, downy mildew symptoms and sanitation.

proposedDescription: Cabbage belongs to a remarkably varied species that also includes kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi. Centuries of cultivation have emphasized different parts of the same basic plant: leaves, flower buds or swollen stems. The leaves are usually thick and waxy, often blue-green, and flowering plants carry yellow, four-petaled blossoms followed by long pods. Wild cabbage and garden forms may look quite different, so a tight leafy head is only one possible expression of this species.
identification: Thick, waxy leaves, yellow cross-shaped flowers and elongated seedpods; cultivated forms vary widely in shape.
actions: Identify volunteers before removal. Rotate vegetable beds and remove unwanted plants before pods split if reseeding is a concern.

sources.title: University of Wisconsin: Growing cole crops

researchNotes: Species-wide overview; not restricted to headed cabbage. No invasive designation inferred from a food crop's presence in the catalog.

claims: Waxy leaves, cultivar variation, yellow four-petaled flowers and splitting pods.
Cultivated groups within B. oleracea and crop rotation to limit soil pathogens.

proposedDescription: Cabbage webworm is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on cabbage and other mustard-family plants. The larvae are pale gray-yellow with several darker stripes running lengthwise, and they shelter in silk among the young leaves. Feeding near the growing point is particularly damaging: young plants may be stunted or develop several small heads instead of one normal head. The adults are brownish moths with pale wing markings, but closely related webworms can look very similar.
identification: Striped larvae and silk webbing around brassica growing points; moth appearance alone does not reliably separate related Hellula species.
actions: Inspect young transplants and growing tips for webbing and caterpillars, and seek local crop advice before treating hidden infestations.

sources.title: University of Hawaii Crop Knowledge Master: Hellula undalis
University of Georgia IPM: Cabbage webworm

researchNotes: UGA account jointly covers H. rogatalis and H. undalis (with a spelling error); its shared traits are not represented as species-exclusive.

claims: Larval stripes, brassica hosts, concealed feeding and young-plant monitoring.
Larval webbing, adult wing pattern and similarity of H. undalis and H. rogatalis.

proposedDescription: Cabbage-stem flea beetles feed on wild and cultivated members of the mustard family. Adults chew the leaves, while their larvae tunnel inside leaf stalks and stems, so the same pest can cause damage in two quite different places. The beetles are usually shiny metallic blue with orange-red legs, although pale and mixed-color forms occur. They are especially important in oilseed rape, where heavy feeding on newly emerged seedlings can destroy the growing point before plants have a chance to recover.
identification: Small beetle about 3-4.5 mm long, usually metallic blue with orange-red legs; pale larvae mine brassica stems and leaf stalks.
actions: Monitor emerging brassica crops for feeding and inspect stems if growth weakens; use local pest thresholds and advice rather than spraying on appearance alone.

sources.title: AHDB: Cabbage stem flea beetle in oilseed rape

researchNotes: Sources use Psylliodes chrysocephala; catalog spelling/ID unchanged. UK crop impacts are not recast as universal US conditions.

claims: Adult size and variable colors, host family and larval stem/petiole mining.
Adult feeding damage, seedling vulnerability and destroyed growing points.

proposedDescription: Cactus moth caterpillars live together inside prickly pear pads, hollowing them out as they feed. Older larvae are bright orange-red with dark bands, a striking contrast to the unobtrusive gray-brown adult moth. Females stack eggs into slender sticks that can resemble cactus spines. Introduced from South America to control unwanted cacti in some countries, the moth became a threat where native prickly pears are important parts of the landscape. Infested pads may yellow, ooze fluid and shed piles of insect droppings.
identification: Orange-red, dark-banded larvae inside cactus pads; spine-like egg sticks and leaking, hollowed pads.
actions: Do not move suspect cacti. Photograph the damage and report it to a state plant-health authority for identification and disposal guidance.

sources.title: USDA APHIS: South American cactus moth

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Grouped internal feeding, larvae, egg sticks, pad symptoms and do-not-move/report guidance.
South American origin, biological-control history, native-cactus threat and adult identification limits.

proposedDescription: The small white butterflies visiting a vegetable patch may be the parents of imported cabbageworms. Their velvety green caterpillars blend into cabbage, broccoli, and related crops, often resting along a leaf vein before chewing holes between the veins. Older larvae do most of the damage and can work their way into developing heads. A regular look beneath the leaves can catch them early; handpicking caterpillars and using well-fitted row covers are useful options for a home garden.
identification: White adults have dark forewing markings. Caterpillars are soft-looking green with faint yellow lengthwise lines, reaching about an inch.
actions: Inspect both leaf surfaces, handpick larvae, and fit row covers before butterflies lay eggs; remove spent crop debris.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Green larvae feed on cole crops and rest along leaf veins.
White adults have black markings; green larvae damage leaves and heads; handpicking and row covers are management options.

proposedDescription: Cadelle beetles live among stored grain and other dry foods, where both the insects and the places they hide deserve attention. The shiny dark adults have a noticeable narrow waist behind the front part of the body; the pale larvae have a black head and dark markings. Feeding damages grain kernels, especially the germ. Larvae can also bore into nearby wood or plaster, creating sheltered places that make an infestation harder to clear. Old grain residues and damaged storage surfaces are useful places to inspect.
identification: Adults are shiny brown to black with a distinct constriction behind the thorax. Larvae are whitish with a black head and dark rear projections.
actions: Isolate affected stored goods, remove old residues, and have storage structures and remaining grain assessed before reuse.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Adults have a distinct waist; larvae and adults damage grain and bore into wood.
Adults measure 6–11 mm; larvae are pale with black markings; old residues and wooden structures shelter infestations.

proposedDescription: Caesarweed has small pink flowers that look like miniature hibiscus blooms, but its hooked fruits are often the more memorable feature. They cling to clothing and animal fur, carrying seeds away from the parent shrub. Rough, sometimes lobed leaves and hairy stems help distinguish it before fruit forms. This widespread tropical plant grows in disturbed places, pastures, and forest openings; Florida treats it as invasive. Brush seeds from clothing and equipment before leaving a patch, and keep seed-bearing cuttings contained during removal.
identification: Look for alternate rough leaves, often shallowly lobed, pink flowers with darker centers, and burr-like fruits that split into five parts.
actions: Remove attached burrs before leaving the site; contain fruiting material and seek local guidance for established patches.
researchNotes: Both sources were read. Origin is described inconsistently or as obscure, so no precise native range is asserted.

claims: Florida lists the shrub as invasive; leaves are rough and flowers pink with darker bases.
Hooked fruits cling to clothing and fur; the shrub occurs in pastures and disturbed forests; origin is obscure.

proposedDescription: Sweet flag grows at wetland edges in clumps of upright, sword-shaped leaves. A short, fleshy spike of tiny flowers appears to project from the side of a leaflike stalk, an unusual feature worth photographing. Names matter here: introduced Acorus calamus has often been confused in North American records with the native American sweet flag, Acorus americanus. The introduced form described by the sources spreads through rhizomes and is sterile. Have a wetland plant specialist confirm the identification before removing a stand or moving divisions.
identification: Photograph the leaf veins and the fingerlike flower spike. The introduced form generally has one strong midvein; native American sweet flag has additional prominent veins.
actions: Leave uncertain wetland plants in place and request a specialist identification before control or transplanting.
researchNotes: Taxonomic conflation is material: retain catalog ID, distinguish A. americanus, and do not transfer all historic occurrence records to introduced A. calamus.

claims: Introduced sterile calamus differs from native fertile American sweet flag in prominent leaf veins.
Historic records conflate native and introduced taxa; introduced triploid plants spread vegetatively.

proposedDescription: Oval-leaved privet is a dense hedge shrub with glossy leaves, fragrant white flower clusters, and small fruits that ripen dark purple-black. Its foliage usually remains through mild winters, giving an escaped plant the same tidy-looking greenery as a garden hedge. The species comes from eastern Asia and is recorded outside cultivation in regional floras. Young shoots are nearly hairless, a useful clue alongside the broad oval leaves. Where seedlings appear beyond a planting, remove them early and prune unwanted flowers before fruit develops.
identification: Check the broad, glossy oval leaves, nearly hairless young shoots, pyramidal clusters of white flowers, and small dark fruits.
actions: Watch the ground beyond hedges for seedlings and prevent unwanted fruiting; confirm local status before choosing a replacement hedge.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Upright shrub has glossy oval leaves, white fragrant panicles and purple-black fruits.
East Asian ornamental hedge shrub occasionally escapes; shoots are nearly hairless and leaves broadly oval.

proposedDescription: California red scale can look like a scattering of tiny reddish-brown disks on citrus leaves, twigs, or fruit. Each disk shelters a sap-feeding insect; newly hatched crawlers move before settling and building their own protective cover. Heavy infestations weaken plants and blemish fruit, but parasitoid wasps often provide valuable control. Look closely before treating a tree, because scale covers can remain after the insect dies. A local crop adviser can help check whether scales are alive and time any treatment to the vulnerable crawler stage.
identification: Female covers are round and reddish-brown, about 2 mm across; male covers are smaller and more elongated.
actions: Inspect foliage, wood and fruit for live scales, preserve natural enemies, and base treatment on monitoring rather than old covers alone.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Round female covers shelter reddish bodies; parasitoids often control the pest and broad insecticides can disrupt them.
Red-brown female covers are about 2 mm; mobile crawlers settle on leaves, shoots and fruit; heavy feeding can cause leaf drop and dieback.

proposedDescription: The white 'flower' of a calla lily is a curved leaflike spathe wrapped around a yellow spike of many tiny flowers. Large arrow-shaped leaves rise from thick underground rhizomes, forming lush clumps in moist ground. This southern African plant is widely grown for gardens and cut flowers. Its ability to grow from rhizomes matters when a planting is removed: leftover pieces should not be dumped beside streams or wetlands. Wear gloves when handling it, and keep the irritating plant material away from children and pets.
identification: Look for broad arrow- to heart-shaped leaves, a white funnel-shaped spathe and a yellow central spike; leaves arise from a fleshy rhizome.
actions: Keep divisions and discarded rhizomes contained, and use gloves when handling this irritating plant.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Southern African rhizomatous plant has arrow-shaped leaves and white spathes; plant parts are poisonous.
Z. aethiopica is the white calla; the showy spathe surrounds true flowers on a fleshy spadix.

proposedDescription: Camellia scale hides beneath small brown, oystershell-shaped covers on the undersides of leaves. Camellias, sasanquas, and hollies are among its hosts, and heavy infestations can make foliage drop. Tiny crawlers briefly move about before settling to feed, while older insects remain protected under their covers. It is easy to confuse this species with other armored scales, so a close photograph or sample is useful. Inspect incoming plants and preserve the lady beetles and parasitic wasps that help keep scale populations down.
identification: Check leaf undersides for narrow brown covers. Male covers are brown, unlike the conspicuous white male covers of tea scale; definitive identification may require microscopy.
actions: Inspect new camellias and hollies, seek confirmation of the scale species, and protect natural enemies when deciding whether treatment is needed.

sources.title: Lepidosaphes tapleyi: comparison with L. camelliae

researchNotes: The Naturalis page is headed L. tapleyi but contains an explicit diagnostic and biological comparison with L. camelliae; only statements assigned to L. camelliae were used.

claims: Brown oystershell covers occur beneath camellia and holly leaves; heavy populations can cause leaf drop; predators and parasitoids attack the scale.
The comparative account explicitly describes L. camelliae as a polyphagous underside-of-leaf scale and a pest of camellia and holly in Florida.

proposedDescription: Camelthorn is a thorny perennial with an underground reach far greater than its modest height suggests. Its stiff branches carry small gray-green leaves and pink to maroon pea flowers; the pods narrow between the seeds like a string of beads. Deep roots and spreading underground stems help it persist in dry ground and colonize irrigated fields or ditch banks. Cutting the top is rarely the end of the job. Keep soil and root fragments from moving to clean areas and plan follow-up with a local weed specialist.
identification: Look for spine-tipped branches, alternate smooth-edged leaves, small pea flowers and strongly constricted seedpods.
actions: Avoid spreading contaminated soil or root pieces; seek a sustained control plan and inspect for regrowth after treatment.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Spiny perennial produces pea flowers and persists through deep spreading roots.
Rhizomes spread far from parent plants; pods are constricted; fragments left in soil can resprout.

proposedDescription: Sometimes called the gas-can beetle, this small ambrosia beetle is drawn to ethanol odors, including those released by stressed trees. Females bore into wood and cultivate fungi that feed their young. The reddish-brown adults are only a few millimeters long, so fresh entry holes and boring dust may attract attention first. Its unusual habit of also boring into some plastic fuel containers explains the nickname. In a landscape, investigate the condition of affected trees and obtain an identification before assuming every tiny hole has the same cause.
identification: Adults are reddish-orange to brown, about 3 mm long, with a hairy, roughened rear end. Small bore holes are clues, not a species-level diagnosis.
actions: Photograph damage and collect a beetle if practical; ask Extension to identify it and assess tree stress before treatment.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Females bore into trees and cultivate fungi; ethanol attraction explains boring into fuel containers.
C. mutilatus females are about 3 mm, reddish-brown with a hairy rough rear; numerous hardwoods are hosts.

proposedDescription: Camphor tree is a broad evergreen with glossy leaves that release a distinctive camphor scent when crushed. Three strong veins often stand out near the leaf base, and small dark fruits attract birds that carry the seeds. Originally from Asia, it can become a large shade tree; in Florida, escaped trees invade disturbed ground and forests. Small seedlings are easier to address than mature trees, which can resprout after cutting. Where it is invasive, choose another shade tree and check nearby woodland for young plants.
identification: Look for alternate glossy leaves with three prominent basal veins, an aromatic crushed leaf and round purple-black fruits.
actions: Where locally invasive, avoid planting it, remove young seedlings, and obtain advice for mature trees because cutting can prompt resprouting.
researchNotes: UF uses Camphora officinarum for this taxon; catalog ID retained. Regional invasive claims are explicitly limited to Florida.

claims: Previously Cinnamomum camphora; Asian evergreen has aromatic leaves and bird-dispersed fruits; invasive in Florida and resprouts after cutting.
Glossy alternate evergreen leaves, small pale flower panicles and dark fleshy fruits characterize the tree.

proposedDescription: Canada bluegrass is a low, spreading perennial whose flattened stems give it another helpful name: flat-stemmed bluegrass. It forms loose turf through underground rhizomes and carries compact, branched seed heads above narrow leaves. Poor, disturbed ground often suits it better than the richer soils favored by some other pasture grasses. Despite its common name, the botanical account treats it as introduced in North America. For an unfamiliar patch, photograph the stem, leaf junction and seed head before deciding how it fits a lawn or restoration site.
identification: Feel for distinctly flattened stems and look for a narrow, contracted panicle and spreading rhizomes.
actions: Confirm the grass from flowering material, then match management to the site; avoid carrying seed or rooted soil into restoration areas.
researchNotes: FEIS header metadata says native but its authored botanical text says introduced. Used the substantive account and flagged the internal inconsistency for reviewer; no nationwide invasive designation inferred.

claims: Botanical text describes an introduced cool-season perennial with flattened stems, long rhizomes and a compressed panicle; it colonizes poor disturbed soils.
Stems are flattened; the flora gives detailed leaf, ligule and panicle characters.

proposedDescription: Canada thistle builds patches from a spreading root system, so the shoots above ground show only part of the plant. Spiny leaves and clusters of small purple flower heads help identify it, but its persistent underground buds explain why a single mowing or digging rarely succeeds. It competes in crops, pastures, and disturbed ground, and livestock often avoid grazing around prickly patches. Prevent seed production, keep root-contaminated soil from moving, and combine repeated follow-up with healthy competing vegetation to gradually weaken an established stand.
identification: Look for upright shoots in spreading patches, sharply spiny leaves and clusters of relatively small purple flower heads.
actions: Prevent seeding and avoid scattering root fragments; use a multiyear plan with repeated follow-up and competitive vegetation.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Root buds drive local spread; tillage fragments can regenerate; persistent integrated management is needed.
Perennial thistle has spiny leaves and purple flowers and spreads by roots.

proposedDescription: Canary Island date palm makes a striking silhouette: a stout trunk topped by a broad crown of long, arching feather leaves. Mature trunks show diamond-shaped scars from old leaf bases, while female trees bear clusters of small yellow-orange dates. Native to the Canary Islands, it is widely planted in warm climates and can naturalize where conditions suit it. The sharp spines at the base of each leaf deserve respect. Leave work high in the crown to a qualified arborist and watch for seedlings beyond the intended planting.
identification: A single thick trunk, diamond-patterned leaf scars, long pinnate leaves and stout spines near the leaf bases distinguish mature trees.
actions: Monitor unwanted seedlings and use a trained arborist for pruning; sharp basal spines make handling fallen or cut leaves hazardous.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Canary Island date palm has a massive trunk and large featherlike leaves; pruning and plant health require care.
Canary Islands native has diamond-shaped trunk scars, spiny leaf bases and yellow-orange fruits; it can naturalize.

proposedDescription: Calico scale earns its name from the white patches on a dark, rounded adult female. These sap-feeding insects settle on deciduous trees, and their sticky honeydew can leave leaves and objects beneath the tree coated with black sooty mold. Young scales spend part of the season on leaves, then move onto twigs to overwinter. A few scales may do little harm, so check the tree's condition as well as the insects. If treatment is needed, monitoring for tiny moving crawlers helps identify the useful window.
identification: Mature females are roughly pea-sized, dark brown or black with conspicuous pale blotches; younger scales are flatter.
actions: Inspect twigs and leaves, assess honeydew and tree vigor, and use local crawler monitoring to time any treatment.
researchNotes: Maryland calls this native while other Extension accounts call it introduced from Asia. Nativity omitted pending editorial taxonomic review; biology corroborated independently.

claims: Females have white patches on dark bodies; feeding causes honeydew, sooty mold and at high levels reduced growth.
One annual generation shifts between leaves and twigs; low populations are not damaging; crawler monitoring guides control.

proposedDescription: Callery pear is conspicuous in spring when clusters of white flowers cover the branches before or around leaf-out. Glossy, rounded leaves follow, along with small hard fruits that birds can carry beyond planted trees. Familiar cultivars such as Bradford belong to this species, and crossing between compatible trees has helped escaped populations spread. Wild seedlings may develop formidable thorns and form dense growth in fields and disturbed places. Replacing a planted tree with a locally appropriate alternative helps reduce seed sources; removal also needs a plan for sprouts.
identification: White spring flower clusters, glossy broad leaves and small round fruits are useful clues; escaped trees often have sharp thorns.
actions: Choose an alternative for new plantings, remove young escapes, and plan follow-up for stump or root sprouts when larger trees are removed.

sources.title: Callery pear: history, identification and control

researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Compatible cultivars produce seed; birds disperse fruits; escaped trees bear thorns and require follow-up control.
White malodorous flowers, glossy alternate leaves, small fruits and brittle branching characterize Callery pear.

proposedDescription: Camphor scale is an armored scale that can hide in plain sight as small brown bumps on ornamental plants. The female's rounded, raised cover usually has a yellow-orange spot toward one side, while the male's cover is more elongated. Despite the common name, its hosts include camellias, citrus, and many other plants as well as camphor trees. Older references call it Aspidiotus duplex; modern accounts use Pseudaonidia duplex. Inspect new plants carefully, and have a sample identified before choosing a scale treatment.
identification: Look for convex brown round or oval covers with an off-center orange-yellow shed skin; authoritative species identification requires a slide-mounted adult female.
actions: Inspect host plants before moving them and consult Extension or a diagnostic laboratory for identification and management.
researchNotes: Catalog ID retained for historical Aspidiotus duplex. ScaleNet and Naturalis are distinct authored syntheses but share some underlying literature; no range claim drawn from conflicting catalogue remarks.

claims: Female covers are convex brown with orange-yellow exuviae; hosts include camphor, camellia and citrus; microscopy is needed.
Aspidiotus duplex is a historical combination; independent cited accounts describe convex female covers and ornamental and citrus pest status.

proposedDescription: Canary Island St. John's wort is a woody shrub with narrow leaves and clusters of bright yellow flowers. Unlike the low-growing St. John's worts many gardeners know, it can reach several meters tall. In coastal California, escaped plantings form dense stands in disturbed grassland and scrub, crowding native vegetation. Both underground spread and abundant seed complicate removal. Photograph the flowers, leaves and stem shape before acting, then work with local land managers to prevent seed production and revisit treated patches for new growth.
identification: A tall shrub with narrow, unstalked leaves, flattened or two-lined stems, yellow flowers and no black glands in the foliage.
actions: Prevent further planting where invasive; confirm identification and arrange repeated follow-up after removing an established patch.
researchNotes: Two independent source accounts opened and read; geographic claims remain limited to the cited sources.

claims: Rhizomatous shrub forms dense stands in coastal California scrub and grassland; prolific seed supports spread.
Shrub reaches 1–4 m, has narrow sessile leaves, compressed stems and yellow flowers without black glands.

proposedDescription: Tall delphinium brings upright spires of blue to purplish flowers above a clump of deeply divided leaves. This perennial comes from Europe and Asia and is the source of many garden selections, so cultivated plants can vary markedly in height and flower color. Its tall stems appreciate shelter and support, especially in wind or heavy rain. Remove spent spikes if you do not want seed, and keep all parts away from grazing animals or curious pets: this beautiful member of the buttercup family is toxic if eaten.
identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves and tall, stiff flower spikes; many garden hybrids differ from the wild species in color and form.
actions: Support tall stems, deadhead unwanted seed production, and prevent children, pets and livestock from eating plant material.
researchNotes: Garden species profile, not evidence of national invasive status. Cultivar variation is acknowledged.

claims: Eurasian perennial has blue flowers, divided leaves, many cultivars and toxic plant material.
Tall perennial bears summer purplish-blue flower spikes; shelter, staking and deadheading are recommended.

proposedDescription: Candlenut, or kukui, is a broad-crowned tropical tree whose pale green foliage can stand out across a wooded valley. Younger leaves are often lobed, while older leaves may be more oval. Small pale flowers give way to rounded fruits enclosing hard, dark seeds rich in oil—the source of the name candlenut. Long valued in Pacific cultures, it is naturalized in Hawaii and holds special cultural significance there. Fallen seeds readily produce seedlings, so watch planting boundaries and avoid distributing unwanted fruit or soil containing seeds.
identification: Look for broad alternate leaves, often lobed when young, pale terminal flower clusters and rounded fruits containing one or two hard dark seeds.
actions: Monitor self-sown seedlings around plantings and contain unwanted seed-bearing material; consider local cultural and land-management context before removal.
researchNotes: Sources use Aleurites moluccanus; exact supplied ID aleurites-moluccanus retained. Cultural importance and naturalization are distinguished from a blanket invasive designation.

claims: Kukui is culturally important and naturalized in Hawaii; oily hard seeds readily germinate.
Broad-crowned tree has alternate leaves often lobed when young, pale flowers and fruits with one or two hard black seeds.

proposedDescription: The New Guinea sugarcane weevil spends its most damaging stage hidden inside a plant. Pale, legless larvae tunnel through sugarcane and palms, often leaving a plug of fibers at a tunnel entrance. Feeding can weaken palm trunks or damage the growing tip, so the first visible sign may be a declining or unstable plant. The species has moved among tropical islands, with transported palms providing a pathway. Keep suspect plants on site and ask an agricultural or plant-health specialist to identify the insect before moving or treating them.
identification: Look for fibrous plugs over tunnels and pale legless grubs inside affected tissue; larvae alone need specialist confirmation.
actions: Do not transport infested palms or cane; seek a diagnosis and current locally approved management advice.
researchNotes: ADAP includes R. asperipennis in shared larval description; species-specific hosts and records were separated. Obsolete mothball treatment in 2000 source intentionally not repeated.

claims: Larvae tunnel inside sugarcane and palms, plug entrances with fibers and can weaken trunks or kill growing tips.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Japan National Institute for Environmental Studies
claims: The weevil affects cane and palms and can hitchhike with transported palm trees.

proposedDescription: Cane toads are large, warty amphibians that often appear around gardens, buildings, and water after dark. Their broad glands behind the eyes can release a milky toxin when threatened, making an encounter dangerous for a pet that bites one. Introduced populations are a management concern in Florida and other warm regions. Smaller native toads can look similar, so size alone is not enough for identification. Keep pet food indoors, supervise pets outside, and photograph an unfamiliar toad before seeking local wildlife guidance.
identification: Look for a large, heavily built brownish toad with conspicuous glands extending behind the eyes; compare carefully with local native species.
actions: Keep pets away, remove outdoor pet food, and seek local identification and humane management advice. Contact a veterinarian promptly if a pet mouths a toad.
researchNotes: Older accounts use a broad R. marina/Bufo marinus concept. Native-range and recent taxonomic split claims omitted; Florida management information retained with geographic context.

evidence.independentSourceGroup: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
claims: Large introduced Florida toad has prominent toxin glands; pet food attracts it; native toad confusion matters.
Warty toad is nocturnal and secretes defensive toxin from large glands.

proposedDescription: Canistel is a tropical fruit tree best known for its golden-yellow fruit and rich, sometimes egg-yolk-like flesh. The glossy leaves are simple and smooth-edged, and small cream flowers sit in their axils. Fruits vary from rounded to spindle-shaped, often ending in a point; several glossy brown seeds lie inside. Garden trees benefit from room to grow and good drainage. Pick fruit at the appropriate mature stage and let it soften before eating, and keep an eye on self-sown seedlings around a planting.
identification: Glossy alternate leaves, small cream flowers and yellow to orange fruits—often pointed—with large brown seeds are useful clues.
actions: Use well-drained planting sites, harvest mature fruit, and remove unwanted volunteer seedlings rather than moving them into natural areas.

sources.title: Canistel growing in the Florida home landscape

researchNotes: Horticultural and botanical profile; consulted sources do not establish broad invasive impacts.

claims: Fruits vary in shape, ripen yellow-orange and contain 1–5 glossy brown seeds; fruit texture changes with ripeness.
Tropical fruit tree has glossy alternate entire leaves and yellow eggfruit.

proposedDescription: Cantaloupes, honeydews, and several less familiar melons all belong to Cucumis melo, a warm-season vine with tendrils, rough leaves, and small yellow flowers. Fruit shape, rind and flesh vary greatly among cultivated groups, so a netted orange-fleshed melon is only one version of the species. Bees and other insects help flowers set fruit. In a garden, give the vines sun, space and well-drained soil, and avoid excess nitrogen that produces lush growth at the expense of fruit.
identification: Trailing or climbing vines bear tendrils, broad rough leaves, yellow flowers and highly variable fleshy fruits; cultivar identity is needed for finer distinctions.
actions: Protect flower-visiting pollinators, provide drainage and room for vines, and remove unwanted volunteers before they set more fruit.

sources.title: Flower and fruit set in cucurbits

researchNotes: Cultivated crop profile; no invasive classification inferred from catalog inclusion.

claims: Cucumis melo includes cantaloupe, honeydew and other cultivar groups with variable fruits; plants are warm-season vines.
Melons depend on insect pollination; excessive nitrogen delays fruiting; muskmelons benefit from well-drained mounds.
